pma-4.19.name: Continuity on a compact space is uniform
pma-4.19.statement: Let $f$ be a continuous map from a compact metric space $X$ into a metric space $Y$. Then $f$ is uniformly continuous on $X$: for every $\eps>0$ there is a single $\delta>0$ such that $d_Y(f(p),f(q))<\eps$ whenever $d_X(p,q)<\delta$.
pma-4.19.caption: Drag the point $p$ and change $\eps$. The lower panel plots the largest admissible $\delta(p)$ at every $p$: on a compact interval its minimum stays positive; on $(0,1]$ it collapses to $0$.

mech-8.22.name: Hamilton’s hodograph: Kepler velocities trace a circle
mech-8.22.statement:
For any orbit in the inverse-square field $F = -k/r^2$, the **hodograph** — the curve traced by the tip of the velocity vector $\mathbf v(t)$ drawn from a fixed origin — is (an arc of) a circle of radius $k/\ell$ (with $\mu = 1$), whose centre lies at distance $e\,k/\ell$ from the origin, perpendicular to the apse line:
$$\mathbf v = \frac{k}{\ell}\,\hat{\mathbf z}\times\big(\hat{\mathbf r} + \mathbf e\big),\qquad \mathbf e = \frac{\mathbf A}{\mu k}.$$
For ellipses ($e<1$) the origin lies inside the circle and the whole circle is traced; for a parabola it lies on it; for hyperbolas it lies outside and only an arc is traced. No other central force law gives a circular hodograph for every orbit.
mech-8.22.caption: Drag the launch point and the tip of the launch velocity. Left: the orbit with velocity arrows at equal time steps. Right: the same arrows drawn from one origin; their tips fall on a circle (a least-squares circle fit is dashed, the gold point is its centre). The readout compares the fitted radius and offset with $k/\ell$ and $ek/\ell$. Launch faster than escape speed: the origin moves outside the circle and only an arc is used. Change the force exponent and the tips leave the circle.

cplx-13.9.name: A Fast Quantum Mechanical Algorithm for Database Search
cplx-13.9.statement:
Given an oracle that recognises one marked item among $N$ unsorted items, a quantum computer can find it with high probability using $O(\sqrt N)$ oracle queries, whereas any classical algorithm needs $\Omega(N)$ (about $N/2$ on average). Starting from the uniform superposition $|s\rangle$, each iteration flips the sign of the marked amplitude and then **inverts every amplitude about the mean**; with $\sin\theta = 1/\sqrt N$, after $k$ iterations the marked item is found with probability
$$P_k = \sin^2\big((2k+1)\theta\big),$$
which is close to 1 after $k \approx \frac{\pi}{4}\sqrt N$ iterations, and falls again if one keeps going. With $M$ marked items, $\sin\theta = \sqrt{M/N}$ and about $\frac{\pi}{4}\sqrt{N/M}$ iterations suffice.

Scope: a quadratic, not exponential, speed-up for unstructured search, and provably optimal: no quantum algorithm can do better than $\Omega(\sqrt N)$ queries (BBBV 1997), so NP-complete problems are not solved in polynomial time this way.
cplx-13.9.caption: **Left**: the amplitudes of all $N$ items as bars (the marked one red; for large $N$ the unmarked items are summarised by one bar, since they stay equal). Drag **iterations** $k$, or press **Step ½** repeatedly: the first press applies only the oracle (the red bar flips sign), the second the inversion about the mean (dashed line). **Middle**: the state as a vector in the plane of $|w\rangle$ and the unmarked superposition, rotating by $2\theta$ per iteration. **Right**: probability of success after $k$ iterations (green) against a classical search that checks one item per query (grey): the quantum curve peaks near $\frac{\pi}{4}\sqrt N$ and then declines. Change $n$ (so $N = 2^n$) and the number $M$ of marked items.

causal-4.4.name: Simpson’s paradox
causal-4.4.credit: Simpson, 1951, JRSS B 13:238–241; Charig et al., 1986, BMJ 292:879–882; Bickel, Hammel & O’Connell, 1975, Science 187:398–404; R datasets UCBAdmissions
causal-4.4.statement: A comparison can reverse when data are pooled: for two groups $a$ and $b$ and strata $s$ it is possible that $P(Y{=}1\mid a,s)>P(Y{=}1\mid b,s)$ in **every** stratum $s$, yet $P(Y{=}1\mid a)<P(Y{=}1\mid b)$ overall, because the groups have different stratum mixes $P(s\mid a)\ne P(s\mid b)$. Arithmetic permits both; **which** comparison answers a causal question depends on the causal graph: if the measured $S$ satisfies the back-door criterion, adjust ($\sum_s P(Y{=}1\mid g,s)P(s)$, 4.3); if $S$ is a mediator, adjustment can remove part of the total effect. A pooled association represents a total causal effect only under additional identification assumptions, such as no unblocked back-door paths.
causal-4.4.caption: Choose a data set: Charig et al.’s kidney-stone counts (open surgery versus percutaneous nephrolithotomy) or the six largest Berkeley departments of 1973 (women versus men). Bars are success or admission rates by stratum and, at the right, pooled; the numbers under each bar are group sizes (denominators). Berkeley is an aggregation contrast: women have higher rates in four of six departments, not every department. Drag **mix shift** to move the first group’s stratum mix toward the second’s (rates unchanged): equal mixes remove the mixing difference, but a sign crossing can occur earlier. At nonzero shift the rounded sizes are synthetic reweighting sizes, not additional observed patients or applicants.

pchem-3.3.name: Carnot cycle and its efficiency
pchem-3.3.statement:
A reversible engine that takes heat $q_h$ from a reservoir at $T_h$, rejects $q_c$ to a reservoir at $T_c$ and delivers the difference as work has efficiency
$$\eta = \frac{w}{q_h} = 1 - \frac{T_c}{T_h},$$
and no engine working between the same two reservoirs can exceed it. For a perfect gas the Carnot cycle consists of an isothermal expansion at $T_h$, an adiabatic expansion down to $T_c$, an isothermal compression at $T_c$ and an adiabatic compression back; in the $T$–$S$ plane it is a rectangle.
pchem-3.3.caption: Drag $T_h$, $T_c$ and the expansion ratio. The pV diagram (one mole of perfect gas) and the TS diagram show the same cycle; the shaded area is the work. Switch on a rival cycle drawn in the TS plane between the same temperature limits and entropy span: its efficiency, computed from the same area ratio, always falls below the Carnot value.

geog-4.4.name: Greenland versus Africa on Mercator
geog-4.4.statement: On a Mercator world map Greenland looks about as large as Africa, yet Africa's area (about 30.4 million km²) is roughly **14 times** Greenland's (about 2.17 million km²). The illusion is exact geometry: Mercator multiplies areas near latitude $\varphi$ by $\sec^2\varphi$, which stays below about 1.6 over nearly all of Africa (35° S to 37° N) but runs from 4 at Greenland's southern tip (60° N) to over 60 on its north coast (83.6° N). Moving Greenland rigidly to the equator on the globe and redrawing it shows its true size relative to Africa.
geog-4.4.caption: Drag the blue copy of Greenland anywhere (or use the buttons). It is moved rigidly on the sphere, so its true area never changes; watch its size on the map shrink as it nears the equator. The corner shows the apparent Greenland : Africa ratio on the map; the right panel plots the area factor $\sec^2\varphi$, with each outline's measured map-to-true ratio as a dot. Switch to Mollweide (equal-area) to see the true proportion everywhere.

mathbio-3.3.name: Lotka–Volterra predator–prey equations
mathbio-3.3.statement:
With prey density $x$ and predator density $y$,
$$\dot x=\alpha x-\beta xy,\qquad \dot y=\delta xy-\gamma y,$$
where prey grow exponentially at rate $\alpha$ when alone, predation removes prey at rate $\beta xy$ (mass action), each prey eaten adds a fraction $\delta/\beta$ to the predators, and predators die at rate $\gamma$ without prey. Besides the unstable saddle $(0,0)$ there is the coexistence equilibrium $(\gamma/\delta,\ \alpha/\beta)$ around which solutions in the open quadrant cycle; for small cycles the period is $2\pi/\sqrt{\alpha\gamma}$.
mathbio-3.3.caption: Units are scaled so that $\beta=\delta=1$, giving the equilibrium $(\gamma,\alpha)$. Drag the gold start point on the phase plane (right) or change $\alpha,\gamma$: the left plot shows prey (blue) and predators (orange) oscillating out of phase, with the lag of the first predator peak after the prey peak measured as a fraction of the period.

imaging-3.3.name: Sinogram
imaging-3.3.statement: The **sinogram** is the Radon transform displayed as an image: one row per view angle $\theta$ (or one column), one pixel per detector element $s$, with grey level equal to the measured line integral. Every object point traces a sinusoidal band of its own, with amplitude equal to its distance from the rotation centre, so the sinogram of a small, off-centre object is a sine wave, one at the centre is a vertical line, and an extended object is the superposition (sum) of such bands. A sinogram that is **not** a sum of sinusoids has been corrupted: if the object moves during the scan the traces break or jump.
imaging-3.3.caption: **Click the left panel** to drop a disc (radius and attenuation from the sliders); the **sinogram** shows its sinusoid and the **reconstruction** (filtered back-projection of the sinogram, 3.7) shows it again. **Clear** starts over. Switch on **patient motion**: after the chosen angle the whole object is shifted, the sinusoids jump, and the reconstruction fills with double edges and streaks.

solid-3.3.name: Mohr’s circle
solid-3.3.statement: For a plane stress state $(\sigma_x,\sigma_y,\tau_{xy})$ plot, in the $(\sigma,\tau)$ plane, the points $X=(\sigma_x,\tau_{xy})$ and $Y=(\sigma_y,-\tau_{xy})$ (the shear component is plotted with the sign of its action on the $x$ face; for $Y$ the sign is reversed). They are the ends of a diameter of a circle with centre $C=\tfrac{\sigma_x+\sigma_y}{2}$ on the $\sigma$-axis and radius $R=\sqrt{(\tfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2})^2+\tau_{xy}^2}$. The state on the faces of an element turned by $\theta$ is the point of the circle reached by rotating $X$ through $2\theta$ **in the opposite sense** when $\tau$ is plotted upward (the same sense as the element when $\tau$ is plotted downward, as in many textbooks). The circle meets the $\sigma$-axis at the principal stresses $C\pm R$.
solid-3.3.caption: Drag the gold point $X'$ around the circle (or use the slider): the element on the left turns by half the angle you sweep, and its stresses are read off the point's coordinates. $X'$ is the state on the $x'$ face, the opposite point $Y'$ is the $y'$ face. The red points on the $\sigma$-axis are the principal stresses and the dashed arc is the angle $2\theta$ from the original point $X$.

macro-3.2.name: The Solow–Swan model
macro-3.2.statement:
A closed economy produces one good with $Y = F(K, L)$ under constant returns, so output per worker is $y = f(k)$ with $k = K/L$, where $f$ is increasing and concave. A fixed fraction $s$ of output is saved and invested, capital depreciates at rate $\delta$, and labour is constant (population growth enters in macro-3.6). Then capital per worker obeys
$$\dot k = s\,f(k) - \delta k .$$
Investment per worker $s f(k)$ adds to the stock, *break-even investment* $\delta k$ replaces what wears out; capital rises where the first exceeds the second and falls where it is smaller. With $f(k) = A k^{\alpha}$ the two curves cross once at $k^* = (sA/\delta)^{1/(1-\alpha)}$.

Scope: a one-good, closed, full-employment economy with a *fixed* saving rate; it explains the level of income, not why technology grows.
macro-3.2.caption: **Left:** the saving curve $s f(k)$ (green) and break-even line $\delta k$ (red); arrows show the direction of motion. Drag the **gold handle** to choose the starting capital per worker $k_0$ and change $s$, $\delta$, $\alpha$ or $A$. **Right:** the path $k(t)$, integrated from the differential equation, with the animated dot; notice how convergence is fast at first and slows near $k^*$.

soc-1.2.name: Schelling’s segregation model
soc-1.2.statement:
Two kinds of agents, blue and orange, occupy the cells of a grid in which some cells are vacant. Each agent looks at its eight surrounding cells and is **content** if at least a fraction $T$ of its occupied neighbours are of its own kind (an agent with no neighbours is content); otherwise it is **discontented**. In each round the discontented move, one at a time in random order, to vacant cells — in the simplest version to any vacancy, in versions closer to Schelling's to a vacancy where they would be content. Rounds repeat until nobody is discontented (or until nobody can move).

The model's output is a spatial pattern and its degree of segregation, measured for instance by the average share of like neighbours, to be compared with the value under random mixing ($s^2 + (1-s)^2$ when a share $s$ of agents is blue).
soc-1.2.caption: Press ▶ (or **Step**) and watch discontented agents relocate. The right panel sorts residents by their share of like neighbours: red residents are below the tolerance line $T$ and will move, purple ones are content; the dashed outline is the starting distribution. The strip below tracks the average like share against the random-mixing level. Click any cell to inspect its neighbourhood. Change $T$ (the run resumes), the vacancies or the blue share (new board), or let movers pick only *a vacancy that suits them*.

art-1.8.name: Two-point perspective
art-1.8.statement:
When a box-shaped object is turned about a vertical axis so that none of its faces is parallel to the picture plane, its vertical edges stay vertical, but its two families of horizontal edges vanish at two points $V_L$, $V_R$ on the horizon: **two-point perspective**. With the eye at distance $d$ from the picture plane and the object turned by $\varphi$ ($0<\varphi<90^\circ$), $V_R$ lies $d\tan\varphi$ to the right of the principal point $P$ and $V_L$ lies $d\cot\varphi$ to its left. Hence
$$\overline{PV_L}\cdot\overline{PV_R}=d^2,$$
and the eye sees the two vanishing points at a right angle. As $\varphi\to 0$ one vanishing point recedes to infinity and the picture becomes one-point (art-1.6).
art-1.8.caption: Drag either vanishing point along the horizon and the building turns. With “keep the eye distance fixed” the other point moves so that $\overline{PV_L}\cdot\overline{PV_R}$ stays $d^2$; switch it off to move them independently, and the eye distance follows. The station point, folded down below the horizon, always sees $V_L$ and $V_R$ at a right angle.

tech-2.9.name: Gear trains and the Antikythera mechanism
tech-2.9.credit: Hellenistic Greek, built c. 2nd century BCE (date disputed); recovered from a shipwreck of c. 70–60 BCE
tech-2.9.statement:
Two meshing gears with $N_1$ and $N_2$ teeth turn in opposite directions with angular speeds in the ratio $N_2 : N_1$. In a **train**, where gears fixed on a common axle form compound stages, the ratios multiply: the output turns $\prod (N_{\text{driver}}/N_{\text{driven}})$ times per turn of the input, so whole-number tooth counts can represent astronomical period relations as exact fractions.

The **Antikythera mechanism**, a hand-cranked bronze calculator recovered in 1901 from a Roman-era wreck off Antikythera, used about thirty gears in this way. In the reconstruction of Freeth et al. (2006), a year's turn of the main wheel drives the **Moon pointer** through the train $64 \to 38,\ 48 \to 24,\ 127 \to 32$, giving
$$\frac{64}{38}\cdot\frac{48}{24}\cdot\frac{127}{32} = \frac{254}{19}$$
sidereal months per year (254 sidereal months ≈ 19 years), and drives the **Metonic** pointer, which runs round a five-turn spiral of 235 lunar months, through $64 \to 38,\ 53 \to 96,\ 15 \to 53$, giving $5/19$ of a turn per year. A pin-and-slot pair of gears made the Moon pointer speed up and slow down, modelling the Moon's varying speed. Freeth et al. (2021) reconstruct the front planetary display (for example Venus with gears 51, 44, 34, 26, 63). The construction date is debated: estimates range from about 205 BCE to about 100 BCE.
tech-2.9.caption: The gears are drawn with their real tooth counts and turn together. Choose the **Moon** or **Metonic** train; time runs at half a year per second from the **start** year (pause and move the slider to scrub). Gears on one axle are drawn concentric; gears working in different planes overlap, as they do in the mechanism. The dial shows the pointer against the Sun pointer (front) or on the 235-month spiral (back). The lower plot is the drift of the pointer from the true Moon or the true lunar months, over a century. **Break it** by changing the big gear's tooth count by one or two and watch the drift take off.

ladr-5.5.name: Eigenvalue
ladr-5.5.statement:
Let $T \in \mathcal L(V)$. A number $\lambda \in \mathbf F$ is an **eigenvalue** of $T$ if there is a vector $v \in V$ with $v \ne 0$ and
$$Tv = \lambda v.$$
ladr-5.5.caption: Drag the unit vector $v$ (gold) around the circle. The red segment is the part of $Tv$ that sticks out of the line through $v$; on the right, the red curve plots it for every direction and the purple curve plots the part along $v$. At a zero of the red curve $Tv = \lambda v$ (green), and the purple curve reads off $\lambda$. The rotation has no real eigenvalue: its red curve never vanishes.

ladr-7.12.name: Eigenvalues of self-adjoint operators are real
ladr-7.12.statement: Every eigenvalue of a self-adjoint operator is real.
ladr-7.12.caption: Drag the entry $T_{12}$ anywhere in $\mathbf C$ (left) and set the real diagonal entries with the sliders. While the Hermitian switch is on, $T_{21}$ is forced to be the mirror image $\overline{T_{12}}$, and the eigenvalues (right, with gold trails) never leave the real axis however you drag. Switch it off and drag $T_{21}$ on its own: the eigenvalues lift off into the complex plane.

ladr-7.29.name: Real spectral theorem
ladr-7.29.caption: Drag $Te_1$ (teal) and $Te_2$ (pink) to edit $T$; in symmetric mode $Te_2$ slides on the dashed guide, which keeps the matrix symmetric. Drag the gold handle $f_1$ to rotate an orthonormal basis $f_1, f_2$ (the dashed arrows are $Tf_1, Tf_2$). The right panel plots the two off-diagonal entries of $\mathcal M(T, (f_1, f_2))$ against the angle of $f_1$. For symmetric $T$ the curves coincide and vanish together; there (the handle snaps) the matrix is diagonal and $f_1, f_2$ lie along the axes of the ellipse $T(\text{unit circle})$. Without symmetry the curves differ by the constant $b - c$, so they never vanish at the same time: the best an orthonormal basis can do is triangular (6.37).

ladr-7.96.name: Ellipsoid with principal axes
ladr-7.96.statement:
Suppose $f_1, \dots, f_n$ is an orthonormal basis of $V$ and $s_1, \dots, s_n$ are positive numbers. The **ellipsoid** $E(s_1f_1, \dots, s_nf_n)$ with **principal axes** $s_1f_1, \dots, s_nf_n$ is the set
$$E(s_1f_1, \dots, s_nf_n) = \Big\{v \in V : \frac{|\langle v, f_1\rangle|^2}{s_1^2} + \cdots + \frac{|\langle v, f_n\rangle|^2}{s_n^2} < 1\Big\}.$$
For example, the ball $B = \{v \in V : \|v\| < 1\}$ equals $E(f_1, \dots, f_n)$ for every orthonormal basis $f_1, \dots, f_n$, by Parseval's identity (6.30).
ladr-7.96.caption: Set the semi-axes with the sliders, aim $f_1$ by dragging its handle (it stays on the unit sphere) and turn $f_2, f_3$ about it; drag the background to rotate the view. The surface is $E(s_1f_1, s_2f_2, s_3f_3)$. Drag the gold point $p$: the bar stacks the three terms $|\langle p, f_k\rangle|^2/s_k^2$, and $p \in E$ exactly when the total stays below the line at $1$. Break orthonormality with the skew slider: the formula now describes a different ellipsoid, whose true axes (green, dashed) differ from the $s_kf_k$, and the tips $s_kf_k$ fall outside it (red dots).

ladr-7.70.name: Singular value decomposition
ladr-7.70.statement:
Suppose $T \in \mathcal L(V, W)$ and the positive singular values of $T$ are $s_1, \dots, s_m$. Then there exist orthonormal lists $e_1, \dots, e_m$ in $V$ and $f_1, \dots, f_m$ in $W$ such that
$$Tv = s_1\langle v, e_1\rangle f_1 + \cdots + s_m\langle v, e_m\rangle f_m$$
for every $v \in V$.
ladr-7.70.caption: Drag the targets $T(1,0)$ and $T(0,1)$ to choose $T$, then watch: the plane (grid, unit circle, face) is first turned so that $e_1, e_2$ lie along the axes, then stretched by $s_1, s_2$ along those axes (with a flip when $\det T < 0$), then turned so that the axes land on $f_1, f_2$. The motion ends exactly on $T$ applied to the picture: the dashed target ellipse is $T(\text{unit circle})$, and $e_k$ arrives at $s_k f_k = Te_k$. Click the timeline to jump to any moment.

fa-12.23.name: The spectral theorem for normal operators
fa-12.23.statement:
If $T\in B(H)$ is normal, there is a unique resolution of the identity $E$ on the Borel subsets of $\sigma(T)$ such that
$$T=\int_{\sigma(T)}\lambda\,dE(\lambda).$$
Furthermore, every $S\in B(H)$ that commutes with $T$ commutes with every $E(\omega)$.
fa-12.23.caption: A normal $3\times3$ operator $T=\sum\lambda_kP_k$ (drag the eigenvalues). For a unit vector $x$ (set its components in the eigenbasis with the sliders), the spectral measure $E_{x,x}$ puts mass $|\langle x,u_k\rangle|^2$ at $\lambda_k$ (dot areas). Then $(Tx,x)=\int\lambda\,dE_{x,x}$ is the **centre of mass** (purple) — it always lies in the convex hull of $\sigma(T)$, the numerical range of a normal operator — and $\norm{Tx}^2=\int|\lambda|^2dE_{x,x}$.

mech-10.8.name: Principal axes of inertia
mech-10.8.statement:
The inertia tensor $\mathsf I$ of a rigid body about any point is real, symmetric and positive semidefinite; it is definite unless all the mass lies on one line through the point. Hence there is an orthonormal basis $\mathbf e_1, \mathbf e_2, \mathbf e_3$ of eigenvectors, the **principal axes**, with real eigenvalues $0 \le I_1 \le I_2 \le I_3$, the **principal moments**. In this basis
$$\mathsf I = \operatorname{diag}(I_1, I_2, I_3), \qquad \mathbf L = (I_1\omega_1,\ I_2\omega_2,\ I_3\omega_3), \qquad T = \tfrac12\left(I_1\omega_1^2 + I_2\omega_2^2 + I_3\omega_3^2\right).$$
Angular momentum is parallel to angular velocity exactly when $\boldsymbol\omega$ lies along a principal axis. If the three moments are distinct, these are the six directions $\pm\mathbf e_i$ and nothing else. If two moments coincide (a symmetric top), every direction in their plane qualifies; if all three coincide (a spherical top), every direction does. The moments obey the triangle inequalities, for instance $I_1 + I_2 \ge I_3$, with equality only for a flat body. Any axis of rotational symmetry of the body is a principal axis.
mech-10.8.caption: Drag the five equal masses and the tip of $\boldsymbol\omega$ (blue); drag the background to rotate. The tensor is diagonalised live, and the three principal axes are drawn through the centre of mass, coloured teal, gold and pink from the smallest moment to the largest. Right: for every direction of $\boldsymbol\omega$ (longitude and latitude), the angle between $\boldsymbol\omega$ and $\mathbf L = \mathsf I\boldsymbol\omega$. It is zero only at the six dots $\pm\mathbf e_i$. Drag the blue handle on the map, or press *Slide ω until L ∥ ω*, and it always ends on one of them. *Make it symmetric* sets two moments equal, and the zeros then fill a whole circle.

mech-11.4.name: Normal modes: the generalized eigenvalue problem
mech-11.4.statement:
Let $M$ and $K$ be real symmetric $n\times n$ matrices with $M$ positive definite, and consider $M\ddot{\boldsymbol\eta} + K\boldsymbol\eta = 0$ (11.3). Then:
(a) The trial solution $\boldsymbol\eta = \mathbf a\cos(\omega t-\varphi)$ works exactly when $K\mathbf a = \omega^2M\mathbf a$: the **generalized eigenvalue problem**. Its eigenvalues $\lambda = \omega^2$ are the $n$ roots of $\det(K-\lambda M) = 0$, and they are all real.
(b) There is a basis of eigenvectors $\mathbf a_1,\dots,\mathbf a_n$ (the **normal modes**) that is orthonormal for $M$ and orthogonal for $K$:
$$\mathbf a_i^{\mathsf T}M\mathbf a_j = \delta_{ij},\qquad \mathbf a_i^{\mathsf T}K\mathbf a_j = \lambda_i\,\delta_{ij}.$$
Geometrically, the ellipsoids $\boldsymbol\eta^{\mathsf T}M\boldsymbol\eta = 1$ and $\boldsymbol\eta^{\mathsf T}K\boldsymbol\eta = 1$ are diagonalised simultaneously: the mode directions are conjugate diameters of both.
(c) If $K$ is positive definite (a strict minimum of $V$), every $\lambda_i > 0$, and every solution is a superposition $\boldsymbol\eta(t) = \sum_i A_i\mathbf a_i\cos(\omega_it-\varphi_i)$ with $\omega_i = \sqrt{\lambda_i}$.
The modes are generally **not** orthogonal in the ordinary sense, and the $\omega_i^2$ are not the eigenvalues of $K$, unless $M$ is a multiple of the identity.
mech-11.4.caption: Left: configuration space of a two-degree-of-freedom system. The orange curve is the kinetic ellipse $\boldsymbol\eta^{\mathsf T}M\boldsymbol\eta = 1$; the blue and red curves are the potential ellipses at the levels $\omega_1^2$ and $\omega_2^2$. Each touches the orange ellipse exactly at the mode vectors $\pm\mathbf a_k$, and the dots oscillate along the modes at their own frequencies. Slide the coordinate change: first $\boldsymbol\xi = L^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\eta$ makes the kinetic ellipse a circle, then a rotation lines the modes up with the axes (normal coordinates). Right: the roots of $\det(K-\lambda M)$ are the $\omega_k^2$; the faint curve $\det(K-\lambda I)$ has different roots unless the mass matrix is a multiple of the identity.

music-2.3.name: Standing waves and normal modes
music-2.3.statement:
Two sinusoidal waves of equal amplitude, wavelength and frequency travelling in opposite directions add up to a **standing wave**:
$$\tfrac12\sin(kx-\omega t)+\tfrac12\sin(kx+\omega t)=\sin kx\,\cos\omega t .$$
Its shape $\sin kx$ never moves; it only swells and shrinks. The points where $\sin kx=0$ (**nodes**, half a wavelength apart) never move, and the points halfway between (**antinodes**) swing the most. On a string fixed at $x=0$ and $x=L$ the ends must be nodes, so $kL=n\pi$: the string fits a whole number $n$ of half-wavelengths, $\lambda_n=2L/n$. These standing waves, $y_n=\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}\cos\omega_nt$, are the string's **normal modes**: motions in which every point oscillates at one frequency, in phase or in antiphase.

If the two waves differ in frequency, the pattern is not standing: the nodes drift and the ends can no longer stay at rest.
music-2.3.caption: Orange runs right, purple runs left, blue is their sum; green dots mark the nodes. Choose the mode number $n$ and listen to it alone. Then **detune** the left-running wave: the nodes start to drift (follow them in the space–time diagram below, where the nodes are the thin dashed lines), the red markers show the ends being dragged off zero, and *Listen* now beats at the difference frequency. Only $\delta=0$ fits a string with fixed ends.

music-2.6.name: The harmonic series
music-2.6.statement: The **harmonic series** on a fundamental $f_1$ is the sequence of frequencies $f_1,2f_1,3f_1,4f_1,\dots$, the mode frequencies of an ideal string (2.4) and the partials of every periodic sound. Harmonic $n$ lies $1200\log_2 n$ cents above the fundamental: the series climbs by an octave (2), a fifth (3:2), a fourth (4:3), a major third (5:4), a minor third (6:5), …, and successive harmonics crowd together, the step from $n$ to $n+1$ being $1200\log_2\frac{n+1}n$ cents. Harmonics $1,2,4,8,16$ are octaves of the fundamental; $3$, $5$, $9$, $15$ lie within a few cents of equal-tempered notes, but $7$ is about 31 ¢ flat of the nearest key, $11$ about 49 ¢ (halfway between two keys) and $13$ about 41 ¢ sharp of its nearest key: no keyboard has these pitches.
music-2.6.caption: Top: harmonics 1–16 of the chosen fundamental on a logarithmic axis above a piano keyboard; they crowd together as they rise, and the gold keys are the nearest piano keys. Bottom: the same harmonics on a staff, with their deviation from the written note in cents (red when the gap is large). Click a harmonic (in either panel) to hear it. *Harmonics 1 → 16* plays the series; *4 : 5 : 6 : 7* plays four harmonics as a chord, and switching on **nearest piano keys** replaces every pitch with its equal-tempered neighbour, so you can compare the two.

pma-8.10.name: Orthonormal systems and Fourier coefficients
pma-8.10.statement:
A sequence $\{\phi_n\}$ of complex functions on $[a,b]$ is an **orthogonal system** if $\int_a^b\phi_n\overline{\phi_m}\,dx=0$ whenever $n\ne m$, and **orthonormal** if in addition $\int_a^b|\phi_n|^2dx=1$ for all $n$. For example, $\{(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{inx}\}$ is orthonormal on $[-\pi,\pi]$. If $\{\phi_n\}$ is orthonormal and
$$c_n=\int_a^b f(t)\overline{\phi_n(t)}\,dt,$$
then $c_n$ is the $n$-th **Fourier coefficient** of $f$ relative to $\{\phi_n\}$, and one writes $f(x)\sim\sum c_n\phi_n(x)$, the **Fourier series** of $f$ (with no claim of convergence).
pma-8.10.caption: The grid shows the Gram matrix $\bigl(\int_a^b\phi_n\overline{\phi_m}\bigr)_{n,m}$ of eight functions, computed by numerical integration: an orthonormal system gives the identity. The monomials $1,x,\dots,x^7$ on $[0,1]$ are far from orthogonal; switch on Gram–Schmidt to turn them into an orthonormal system (shifted Legendre polynomials).

pma-8.11.name: Partial Fourier sums are the best mean-square approximations
pma-8.11.statement:
Let $\{\phi_n\}$ be orthonormal on $[a,b]$ and let $s_n=\sum_{m=1}^n c_m\phi_m$ be the $n$-th partial sum of the Fourier series of $f$. If $t_n=\sum_{m=1}^n\gamma_m\phi_m$ is any other combination of $\phi_1,\dots,\phi_n$, then
$$\int_a^b|f-s_n|^2\,dx\le\int_a^b|f-t_n|^2\,dx,$$
with equality only when $\gamma_m=c_m$ for $m=1,\dots,n$.
pma-8.11.caption: Here $n=2$ with $\phi_1=\frac{\sin x}{\sqrt\pi}$, $\phi_2=\frac{\sin 2x}{\sqrt\pi}$ on $[-\pi,\pi]$. Drag $\gamma=(\gamma_1,\gamma_2)$ on the right: the colour is the error $\int|f-t_2|^2$, a paraboloid whose level sets are circles about the Fourier coefficients $c=(c_1,c_2)$ (green). Left: $f$, your $t_2$ (gold, error shaded) and $s_2$ (green). The readout checks the Pythagorean identity numerically.

rca-9.13.name: The Plancherel theorem
rca-9.13.caption: Choose $f$ — $\frac{\sin x}{x}$ is in $L^2$ but not in $L^1$, so $\hat f$ cannot be defined by an integral — and move the cut-off $A$. Left: $f$ with the window $[-A,A]$. Right: the transforms $\varphi_A$ of the truncations (blue) approaching the Plancherel transform $\hat f$ (green) in the mean, while the Gibbs overshoot persists. Bottom: four norms computed independently — two in space, two in frequency (on $|t|\le400$). They agree pairwise, as (b) predicts, and the error pair shrinks to $0$, as (d) predicts.

music-4.2.name: Fourier series of a periodic tone
music-4.2.credit: Joseph Fourier, 1807–1822; Dirichlet, 1829; Ohm and Helmholtz brought it to hearing, 1843–1863
music-4.2.statement:
Let $p(t)$ be the pressure of a steady tone with period $T=1/f_0$, integrable over a period. Its **Fourier coefficients** are
$$c_n=\frac1T\int_0^Tp(t)\,e^{-2\pi inf_0t}\,dt,\qquad A_n=2|c_n|,\quad \varphi_n=\arg c_n\quad(n\ge1),$$
and its partial sums are
$$S_Np(t)=c_0+\sum_{n=1}^{N}A_n\cos(2\pi nf_0t+\varphi_n).$$
(a) If $p$ has finite energy over a period, then $S_Np\to p$ in mean square: $\frac1T\int_0^T|p-S_Np|^2\,dt\to0$.
(b) If $p$ is piecewise smooth, then $S_Np(t)\to\tfrac12\big(p(t^-)+p(t^+)\big)$ at every $t$. The convergence is uniform on closed intervals where $p$ is continuous, and uniform everywhere if $p$ is continuous.

So a periodic tone is a sum of **harmonics** at the whole multiples $nf_0$ of its repetition rate, with amplitudes and phases fixed by the waveform. No other frequencies can occur.
music-4.2.caption: Choose a waveform, or **draw** one: drag across the right half of the top panel (the first period; the second repeats it). On the left, $N$ phasors of lengths $A_n$ turn at $n$ times the fundamental rate, chained tip to tail. Their height is the partial sum (blue), traced through time against the target (dashed); red shading marks the error. Below are the amplitudes and phases the waveform implies. Raise $N$ and *Listen* (or hold the tone) to hear the sum close in on the waveform. *Build up* plays $N$ = 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 40 in turn.

algo-4.11.name: Fast Fourier transform (Cooley–Tukey)
algo-4.11.statement:
For $n$ a power of 2, the **fast Fourier transform** computes $y=\mathrm{DFT}_n(a)$ recursively. Split $A(x)=A^{[0]}(x^2)+x\,A^{[1]}(x^2)$, where $A^{[0]}$ has the even-indexed and $A^{[1]}$ the odd-indexed coefficients; compute $y^{[0]}=\mathrm{DFT}_{n/2}(a_0,a_2,\dots)$ and $y^{[1]}=\mathrm{DFT}_{n/2}(a_1,a_3,\dots)$ recursively, and combine with $n/2$ **butterflies**
$$y_k=y^{[0]}_k+\omega_n^k\,y^{[1]}_k,\qquad y_{k+n/2}=y^{[0]}_k-\omega_n^k\,y^{[1]}_k,\qquad 0\le k<n/2 .$$
It uses $\tfrac n2\lg n$ complex multiplications and $n\lg n$ complex additions, so $T(n)=2T(n/2)+\Theta(n)=\Theta(n\log n)$ instead of $\Theta(n^2)$.
algo-4.11.caption: Step through the recursion (the tree shows which coefficients each call receives; gold = running, orange = on the call stack, green = returned). At each butterfly the plane shows $y^{[0]}_k$ (blue), the twisted odd value $t=\omega_n^k y^{[1]}_k$ (purple) added and subtracted at its tip, and the two outputs $y_k$ (green) and $y_{k+n/2}$ (teal); earlier butterflies of the same call stay faint. Right: complex multiplications, the FFT's $\tfrac n2\lg n$ against the $n^2$ of the definition.

thermo-5.6.name: Boltzmann entropy
thermo-5.6.credit: L. Boltzmann, 1870s (entropy–probability relation); M. Planck, c. 1900 (the form $S=k\ln W$ and the constant $k$)
thermo-5.6.statement: The (Boltzmann) entropy of an isolated system in the macrostate with multiplicity $\Omega$ is $S=k\ln\Omega$, where $k=1.380649\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J/K}$ is Boltzmann's constant. Because the multiplicity of two independent systems is the product $\Omega_{AB}=\Omega_A\Omega_B$, the logarithm makes the entropy **additive**, $S_{AB}=S_A+S_B$, and extensive; it also compresses astronomically large counts into numbers of the size of $N$. Given the postulate 5.5, $S$ is the logarithm of the probability weight of a macrostate (up to an additive constant), and its maximisation over unconstrained macrostates is the statistical form of the second law.
thermo-5.6.caption: **Set the size and energy of two Einstein solids** with the sliders. The left panel stacks the entropies $S_A/k=\ln\Omega_A$ and $S_B/k=\ln\Omega_B$ into the entropy of the combined system, whose multiplicity is the product — the stack and the bar for the product agree. The right panel scales one solid with $q=N$ up to a mole: its entropy in J/K grows linearly in $N$, while its multiplicity has about $10^{23}$ digits.

info-1.2.name: Shannon entropy
info-1.2.statement:
The **entropy** of a discrete random variable $X$ with distribution $p(x)=P(X=x)$ on a finite or countable set $\mathcal X$ is its expected surprisal,
$$H(X)=\mathbb E\Big[\log_2\frac1{p(X)}\Big]=-\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}p(x)\log_2 p(x)\qquad\text{bits},$$
with the convention $0\log 0=0$, so outcomes of probability zero contribute nothing. $H$ depends only on the list of probabilities, not on the values of $X$; it is $0$ exactly when $X$ is constant (almost surely), it is at most $\log_2|\mathcal X|$ for a finite alphabet (1.4), and it may be infinite for a countable one. For i.i.d. samples $X_1,X_2,\dots$ the average surprisal $\frac1n\sum_{i\le n}\log_2\frac1{p(X_i)}$ converges to $H(X)$ almost surely, by the law of large numbers.
info-1.2.caption: **Your distribution:** drag the blue bars (pull one to the axis for an exact zero). The numbers above the bars are surprisals; the middle panel stands each outcome's surprisal on a base as wide as its probability, so the green line, the mean height, is $H$. Gold rings show frequencies in the samples, and the running average of their surprisal (bottom) settles on $H$. **English text:** the opening of *Alice in Wonderland*, reduced to 27 symbols (a–z and space). Each symbol is shaded by its surprisal under the frequencies of the first $n$ characters, set by the slider (red: not seen yet, estimated probability $0$); the bottom panel shows how the estimate $\hat H$ settles as more text is read.

thermo-5.16.name: Maxwell’s demon
thermo-5.16.credit: J. C. Maxwell, 1867 (letter to P. G. Tait, 11 December); the name “demon”: W. Thomson, 1874 (Nature 9, 441); C. H. Bennett, 1982 (Int. J. Theor. Phys. 21, 905)
thermo-5.16.statement: Maxwell (1867) imagined a small being at a trapdoor between two chambers of gas at equal temperature that opens only for fast molecules coming from the right and slow ones coming from the left. Without any work, the left chamber would get hotter and the right colder, decreasing the total entropy and apparently violating the second law. The paradox is resolved by treating the demon as a physical system that must acquire and store information about each molecule: its memory fills up, and since a finite memory must eventually be erased, the entropy (at least $k\ln2$ per bit, 5.17) dumped into the environment by erasure more than compensates the entropy decrease of the gas. A demon that only measures and discards the result gives no net benefit: the second law holds for demon plus gas plus memory.
thermo-5.16.caption: **Press play** with the demon active: it records one bit for every molecule that arrives at the door and lets fast ones pass right-to-left and slow ones left-to-right. The middle panel follows the two temperatures. The right panel is the entropy ledger in units of $k$: the gas entropy change (small and negative), the demon's memory ($+\ln2$ per bit), and — after *Erase memory* — the heat sent to the surroundings. The total is never negative. Switch the demon off and the door simply stays open: the temperatures remain equal.

thermo-5.17.name: Landauer’s principle
thermo-5.17.credit: R. Landauer, 1961 (IBM J. Res. Dev. 5, 183–191); experimental test with a colloidal particle in a double well: A. Bérut et al., 2012 (Nature 483, 187)
thermo-5.17.statement: Erasing one bit of information — resetting a memory that may hold 0 or 1 to a standard value — in an environment at temperature $T$ necessarily dissipates heat $Q\ge kT\ln2$ into that environment, i.e. increases the entropy of the surroundings by at least $k\ln2$. More generally, any logically irreversible operation that reduces the entropy of the memory by $\Delta S$ releases at least $T\,|\Delta S|$. The bound can be approached by quasi-static (slow) protocols and is exceeded by finite-time ones. At $T=300$ K, $kT\ln2=2.87\times10^{-21}$ J $=0.0179$ eV.
thermo-5.17.caption: **Choose the protocol duration $\tau$** (in units of the time a particle takes to diffuse across a well) and press play. The memory is a particle in a double well $V=\tfrac14ax^4-\tfrac12m(t)x^2+f(t)x$ with a barrier of $8\,kT$: the barrier is lowered, the wells tilted toward the left, the barrier restored, the tilt removed. The distribution $p(x)$ is evolved by the Fokker–Planck equation, so the work $W=\int\langle\partial_tV\rangle dt$ is exact. Right: the heat released against $\tau$, with the bound $kT\,|\Delta S|$ (green) from the entropy actually removed and $kT\ln2$ (orange).

info-2.1.name: Relative entropy (Kullback–Leibler divergence)
info-2.1.statement:
Let $p$ and $q$ be probability distributions on the same finite alphabet. The **relative entropy** (Kullback–Leibler divergence) of $p$ from $q$ is
$$D(p\,\|\,q)=\sum_x p(x)\log_2\frac{p(x)}{q(x)},$$
with the conventions $0\log\frac0q=0$ and $p\log\frac p0=+\infty$ for $p>0$. So $D(p\|q)=\infty$ whenever $q$ rules out an outcome that $p$ allows. It is not a distance: in general $D(p\|q)\neq D(q\|p)$, and the triangle inequality fails. It is the expected log-likelihood ratio $\mathbb E_p\log\frac{p(X)}{q(X)}$, the average evidence per sample, in bits, that data from $p$ give *against* the hypothesis $q$.
info-2.1.caption: Drag the blue bars ($p$, the truth) and the orange bars ($q$, the belief). The third panel shows the terms of $D(p\|q)$ (blue) and of $D(q\|p)$ (orange); red bars are negative terms. The presets show $q$ missing an outcome of $p$ (then $D(p\|q)=\infty$ but $D(q\|p)$ is finite) and the reverse.

deep-1.9.name: Softmax and cross-entropy loss
deep-1.9.statement:
For a classifier with $K$ classes the network outputs **logits** $z\in\R^K$, turned into probabilities by the **softmax**
$$p_k=\operatorname{softmax}(z)_k=\frac{e^{z_k/T}}{\sum_{j=1}^Ke^{z_j/T}}\qquad(T=1\text{ by default; }T>0\text{ is the temperature}),$$
a smooth map onto the interior of the probability simplex. It is invariant under adding the same constant to every logit, $\operatorname{softmax}(z+c\mathbf 1)=\operatorname{softmax}(z)$, approaches the indicator of $\arg\max z$ as $T\to0$ and the uniform distribution as $T\to\infty$. The **cross-entropy loss** of a label $y$ is the negative log-likelihood of the categorical model,
$$\ell(z,y)=-\log p_y=-z_y+\log\sum_j e^{z_j},$$
the cross-entropy $H(e_y,p)$ between the one-hot distribution and $p$; its gradient in the logits is $p-e_y$ (3.6).
deep-1.9.caption: Left: drag the three logits. Middle: the softmax probabilities, the true label's bar outlined, with the cross-entropy $-\log p_y$. Right: the probability simplex; the gold point is $p$, the curve is the path of $p$ as the temperature runs from $0.05$ to $20$ (towards a vertex and towards the centre), and the lines are levels of the cross-entropy. *Add 1 to every logit* moves the bars on the left but nothing else.

top-3.17.name: Every self-map of an interval has a fixed point
top-3.17.statement: If $f\colon[0,1]\to[0,1]$ is continuous, there is $x\in[0,1]$ with $f(x)=x$. The same holds for any closed bounded interval, and fails for the interval with a point removed.
top-3.17.caption: Drag the six gold nodes (the graph is a smooth interpolation between them, always inside the square): every crossing with the dashed diagonal is a fixed point, found by bisection on $g(x)=f(x)-x$ and marked in green. Switch on "remove the point $a$": the map on $[0,1]\setminus\{a\}$ drawn in red sends each piece into the other piece, is continuous, and has no fixed point.

pma-9.23.name: Contraction principle (Banach fixed point theorem)
pma-9.23.statement: If $X$ is a complete metric space and $\varphi$ is a contraction of $X$ into $X$, then there is one and only one $x\in X$ with $\varphi(x)=x$.
pma-9.23.caption: Choose a space and a map, drag the starting point $x_0$ and set the number of steps $n$. The right panel plots $\log_{10}$ of the step lengths $d(x_{k+1},x_k)$ (gold) and of the errors $d(x_k,x^*)$ (green dots) against $k$, with the a priori bound $c^k d(x_1,x_0)/(1-c)$ from the proof (dashed): geometric decay, i.e. straight lines of slope $\log_{10}c$. In the plane the dashed circle about $x_n$ has that radius and always contains $x^*$. The last two examples break completeness and the condition $c<1$.

ode-2.4.name: Picard–Lindelöf theorem
ode-2.4.statement: Let $f$ be continuous on the box $R=\{|t-t_0|\le a,\ |x-x_0|\le b\}\subset\R\times\R^n$ and Lipschitz in $x$ on $R$ with constant $L$. Put $M=\max_R|f|$ and $\delta=\min(a,b/M)$. Then the initial value problem $\dot x=f(t,x)$, $x(t_0)=x_0$ has exactly one solution on $[t_0-\delta,t_0+\delta]$. Equivalently, the Picard map $P\varphi=x_0+\int_{t_0}^tf(s,\varphi(s))\,ds$ is a contraction on the complete metric space $C([t_0-\delta,t_0+\delta])$ with the weighted norm $\|u\|_w=\sup_t e^{-2L|t-t_0|}|u(t)|$, with contraction factor $\tfrac12$.
ode-2.4.caption: Drag the two blue handles on the left edge: two different constant initial guesses. Both are pushed through the Picard map $k$ times. The right panel plots their distance in the sup norm (it may grow at first if $LT>1$, then collapses factorially) and in the weighted norm (it shrinks by at least $\tfrac12$ every step, always). For $\dot x=x^2$ the Lipschitz constant is only local: make the interval long and the weighted ratio (measured with $L$ on the region the iterates visit) stops being tidy.

game-2.3.name: Nash’s existence theorem
game-2.3.credit: John F. Nash, Jr., 1950 (Kakutani proof); 1951 (Brouwer proof)
game-2.3.statement:
Every finite strategic game — finitely many players, each with finitely many actions, arbitrary payoffs — has at least one Nash equilibrium in mixed strategies. Equivalently, the product of simplices $\Delta=\prod_i\Delta(A_i)$ contains a profile $\sigma^*$ such that $U_i(\sigma^*)\ge U_i(\tau_i,\sigma^*_{-i})$ for every player $i$ and every mixed $\tau_i$. Nash's second proof defines the continuous map $f:\Delta\to\Delta$,
$$f(\sigma)_{i}(a)=\frac{\sigma_i(a)+g_i^a(\sigma)}{1+\sum_{b}g_i^b(\sigma)},\qquad g_i^a(\sigma)=\max\bigl\{0,\;U_i(a,\sigma_{-i})-U_i(\sigma)\bigr\},$$
whose fixed points are exactly the equilibria; Brouwer's theorem gives a fixed point. Existence is all that is asserted: the equilibrium need not be unique, and iterating $f$ need not converge to it.
game-2.3.caption: Each triangle is a simplex of mixed strategies of a $3\times3$ game (corners are pure actions): row player on the left, column player on the right. Drag the two gold starting points; the slider runs $n$ steps of Nash's map and draws the orbit. Green rings are all equilibria, found independently by solving every support. Whenever the orbit settles, it is on a green ring, and the regret curve (log scale) falls to zero. Not every game obliges — try the Rock–Paper–Scissors-type game and the *best-reply jump* map, which cycles forever.

stoch-4.15.name: PageRank
stoch-4.15.statement:
Given a directed graph of $n$ pages, let $M$ be the link matrix of the surfer who follows a uniformly random outgoing link (a page without links jumps to a uniformly random page), and let $d\in[0,1)$ be the damping factor. The **PageRank** vector is the stationary distribution of the chain
$$G=d\,M+(1-d)\tfrac1n\mathbf 1\mathbf 1^{\!\top}.$$
Because every entry of $G$ is at least $(1-d)/n>0$, the chain is irreducible and aperiodic; so the stationary distribution $r$ exists and is unique (4.4), every start converges to it (4.7), and the power iteration $r_{k+1}=r_kG$ satisfies $\|r_k-r\|_1\le 2d^{\,k}$.
stoch-4.15.caption: Edit the web: click empty space to add a page, click one page then another to add a link (Alt-click removes). The notes on the pages are their rank after $k$ power-iteration steps from the uniform start. Middle: the rank vector at step $k$ (bars) against the exact stationary law (dots). Right: the $\ell^1$ error on a log scale, falling below the guaranteed $2d^k$ (dashed). Lower $d$ makes convergence faster but flattens the ranking towards uniform; $d\to1$ approaches the raw link-following chain.

mech-5.2.name: Fermat’s principle and Snell’s law
mech-5.2.credit: Hero of Alexandria (reflection, c. 60); Fermat, 1662; Snell, 1621
mech-5.2.statement:
**Fermat's principle.** Between two points, light travels along a path that makes the travel time $\displaystyle T=\int\frac{ds}{v}=\frac1c\int n\,ds$ stationary (in simple situations, a minimum), where $v=c/n$ is the local speed of light and $n$ the refractive index.
**Snell's law** follows: when light crosses a flat interface from a medium of index $n_1$ into one of index $n_2$, the angles $\theta_1,\theta_2$ from the normal satisfy
$$n_1\sin\theta_1=n_2\sin\theta_2\qquad\Big(\text{equivalently}\ \frac{\sin\theta_1}{v_1}=\frac{\sin\theta_2}{v_2}\Big).$$
Through a stack of parallel layers the quantity $n\sin\theta$ is the same in every layer.
mech-5.2.caption: *Two media*: drag the blue crossing point along the interface (or move $S$ and $P$). The right panel plots the travel time of every such path; your path is the gold dot and the green dot is the true minimum found numerically — it sits exactly where $n_1\sin\theta_1=n_2\sin\theta_2$ (dashed line). *Stack of layers*: drag the crossing points on all four interfaces; the bars show $n\sin\theta$ in each layer, and *Least-time path* relaxes them — at the minimum all bars have the same height.

mech-5.7.name: Brachistochrone: the cycloid
mech-5.7.credit: Johann Bernoulli, 1696; solved by him, Jakob Bernoulli, Leibniz, Newton and L’Hôpital, 1697
mech-5.7.statement:
A bead slides without friction, starting from rest, along a wire from $A$ to a lower point $B$ not directly below it, in uniform gravity $g$. Measure $y$ downward from $A$. The travel time is
$$T[y]=\int_0^{x_B}\sqrt{\frac{1+y'^2}{2g\,y}}\;dx ,$$
and among all curves joining $A$ to $B$ it is least for the **cycloid**
$$x=R(\theta-\sin\theta),\qquad y=R(1-\cos\theta),\qquad 0\le\theta\le\theta_B,$$
traced by a point on a circle of radius $R$ rolling under the horizontal line through $A$; $\theta_B$ and $R$ are fixed by passing through $B$, and the minimal time is $T=\theta_B\sqrt{R/g}$. The cycloid starts vertically, and if $x_B/y_B>\pi/2$ it dips below $B$ and climbs back up to it.
mech-5.7.caption: Press play: five beads race from A to B in slow motion, each simulated by integrating $\ddot s = -g\,dy/ds$ along its wire. Drag B to change the target (far and shallow, and the winning cycloid dips below B), and drag the two orange points to shape your own curve. The bars rank the simulated finish times; the readout checks them against the quadrature $\int ds/v$ and the cycloid's closed form.

mech-5.4.name: Euler–Lagrange equation
mech-5.4.statement:
Let $f(x,y,p)$ be $C^2$ and let $y\in C^2[a,b]$ be a stationary point — in particular, any local extremum — of
$$J[y]=\int_a^b f\big(x,y,y'\big)\,dx$$
among $C^1$ functions with the same end values. Then $y$ satisfies the **Euler–Lagrange equation**
$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\big(x,y,y'\big)-\frac{d}{dx}\,\frac{\partial f}{\partial y'}\big(x,y,y'\big)=0\qquad(a\le x\le b).$$
More precisely, for every $C^1$ variation $\eta$ with $\eta(a)=\eta(b)=0$ the **first variation** is
$$\delta J[y;\eta]=\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}J[y+\varepsilon\eta]\Big|_{\varepsilon=0}=\int_a^b\Big(f_y-\frac{d}{dx}f_{y'}\Big)\eta\,dx .$$
mech-5.4.caption: Pick a functional. The green dashed curve solves its Euler–Lagrange equation; the blue candidate is that solution plus a defect — drag the blue point to change it (put it back on the green curve to remove the defect). The gold curve is the candidate pushed by $\varepsilon\eta$. Right: $J(\varepsilon)$ for the chosen direction $\eta$, with the tangent line whose slope is the first-variation formula. The purple curve below is the Euler–Lagrange residual along the candidate: the slope is $\int(\text{residual})\cdot\eta$, zero for every $\eta$ only when the residual vanishes.

mech-7.3.name: Noether’s theorem
mech-7.3.statement:
Let $Q(s,q)$ be a one-parameter family of transformations with generator $K(q) = \partial Q/\partial s|_{s=0}$, under which $L(q,\dot q,t)$ changes, to first order in $s$, by a total derivative: $\delta L = \frac{d}{dt}F(q,t)$. Then along every solution of Lagrange’s equations the **Noether charge**
$$\mathcal Q = \sum_j p_j\,K_j(q) - F, \qquad p_j = \frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q_j},$$
is constant. More generally, for any generator, $\dfrac{d\mathcal Q}{dt} = \delta L - \dot F$ along solutions: the charge drifts at exactly the rate at which the transformation fails to be a symmetry (for translations and rotations, the generalized force or torque along $K$). If the transformation also shifts time, $t\mapsto t + s\,\tau(t)$, the charge acquires the term $-h\,\tau$, with $h$ the energy function (7.6).
mech-7.3.caption: Pick a symmetry. The particle moves in the shaded potential; faint arrows show the generator $K$, the green arrow $K$ at the particle and the purple arrow the force. Slide $\varepsilon$ to $0$: the potential becomes invariant and the charge (right, blue) stays on its starting value (dotted). With $\varepsilon > 0$ the symmetry is broken and the charge drifts — exactly along the dashed curve, the running integral of $\delta L$. In the Kepler mode the charge is the Runge–Lenz vector: fixed for $1/r$, and turning steadily under an extra $1/r^3$ force, while $L_z$ stays exact.

qm-6.4.name: Feynman path integral
qm-6.4.statement:
The propagator of $H=p^2/2m+V(x)$ is the limit of integrals over time-sliced paths,
$$K(x_b,T;x_a,0)=\lim_{N\to\infty}\Big(\frac{m}{2\pi i\hbar\varepsilon}\Big)^{N/2}\!\!\int\!\cdots\!\int e^{\,iS_N[x_0,\dots,x_N]/\hbar}\,dx_1\cdots dx_{N-1},\qquad \varepsilon=\frac TN,\;x_0=x_a,\;x_N=x_b,$$
with the discretised action $S_N=\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}\varepsilon\big[\tfrac m2\big(\tfrac{x_{j+1}-x_j}{\varepsilon}\big)^2-V\big(\tfrac{x_j+x_{j+1}}2\big)\big]$. Every path between the endpoints contributes a unit-modulus phasor $e^{iS/\hbar}$ of equal weight; the amplitude is the (appropriately normalised) sum of all of them. The integrals are oscillatory, not absolutely convergent, and are defined by the limit (or by a convergence factor, equivalently a slight rotation of time into the complex plane); the formula is a principle that reproduces Schrödinger’s equation, not a theorem with a measure behind it.
qm-6.4.caption: Choose a particle (free or oscillator), the number of time slices $N$ and the end point $x_b$. The top-left panel draws random piecewise-linear paths from $x_a$ to $x_b$, coloured by the phase of $e^{iS}$; green is the classical path. The top-right panel adds their phasors: the gold trail is the running average of $e^{iS}$ over paths drawn from a Gaussian cloud of width $W$ around the straight line, times the known constant. To make the sum converge, far-out paths are tapered by that same Gaussian (a convergence factor): the trail closes in on the black target $K_W$ at the rate $1/\sqrt n$ (bottom), and $K_W$ approaches the true kernel $K$ (green) as $W$ grows — but then the phasors cancel ever more, so the noise grows like $W^{N-1}$.

soc-4.2.name: The giant component appears at mean degree one
soc-4.2.statement:
Let $G(n,c/n)$ be the random graph with fixed mean degree $c$ as $n\to\infty$.

(a) If $c<1$, with high probability every component has $O(\log n)$ vertices (all are small trees, essentially).

(b) If $c>1$, there is, with high probability, exactly one component with $\sim S n$ vertices, the **giant component**, where $S\in(0,1)$ is the positive solution of
$$S = 1 - e^{-cS},$$
and every other component has $O(\log n)$ vertices.

(c) At $c=1$ the largest component has size of order $n^{2/3}$.

So the emergence of the giant component is a **phase transition**: the fraction of vertices in the largest component is $0$ for $c\le1$ and grows continuously (like $2(c-1)$ just above 1) afterwards.
soc-4.2.caption: **Left**: the share of vertices in the largest component against $c$ for one growing random graph of $n=100,\,1000,\,10\,000$ vertices (dots/lines) and the limit curve. **Right**: the fixed-point picture: the non-zero crossing of $y=1-e^{-cS}$ with $y=S$ exists only when the slope $c$ at $S=0$ exceeds 1. Drag $c$ across 1 and watch the finite curves sharpen towards the kink.

soc-1.8.name: Granovetter’s threshold model of collective behaviour
soc-1.8.statement:
In Granovetter's threshold model a group of $N$ people faces a binary decision, such as whether to join a riot. Person $i$ has a **threshold** $\theta_i$: the number (or proportion) of others who must already have joined before $i$ will join — the point where, for that person, the benefits of joining begin to exceed the costs. People with $\theta_i = 0$ act regardless (instigators). Let $F(x)$ be the number of people with threshold at most $x$, the cumulative distribution of thresholds.

Starting from nobody, the number acting evolves by $$r(t+1) = F\big(r(t)\big), \qquad r(0) = 0.$$ The sequence never decreases and stops at the equilibrium $r_e$, the smallest $r$ with $F(r) = r$: the point where the cumulative curve first meets the 45° line coming from above. The outcome is determined by the whole distribution of thresholds, not by its average.
soc-1.8.caption: The crowd (left, sorted by threshold, each disc labelled with its threshold) joins round by round: red = rioting, gold ring = joined this round. The middle panel is the cumulative distribution of thresholds against the 45° line, with the cascade as a cobweb. Draw your own distribution by dragging on the histogram at the bottom (people per bin of five threshold values), or load a preset; ▶ replays the cascade.

pde-1.4.name: Diffusion and the heat equation
pde-1.4.statement:
**Conservation law plus Fick/Fourier law.** If $u(x,t)$ is a density (heat content, concentration) that is only moved around, then $\frac{d}{dt}\int_a^bu\,dx=q(a,t)-q(b,t)$ for the flux $q$, hence $u_t=-q_x$. If the flux runs down the gradient, $q=-k\,u_x$ with $k>0$ (Fick's law; Fourier's law for heat), we get the **heat (diffusion) equation** $u_t=k\,u_{xx}$.
**Random walk.** A particle that every $\Delta t$ jumps by $\pm\delta$ with probability $\tfrac12$ each has a probability density $p(x,t)$ that satisfies the same equation with $k=\delta^2/(2\Delta t)$ as $\delta,\Delta t\to0$ with $k$ fixed; started at $0$ it is $p(x,t)=(4\pi kt)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/4kt}$, with variance $\mathbb E x^2=2kt$.
pde-1.4.caption: Walkers all start at $0$ and take a step $\pm\delta$ every $\Delta t$ (run starts again when you change a slider). The histogram is the empirical density; the green curve is the heat-equation solution with $k=\delta^2/2\Delta t$, and the gold dots are the exact master-equation (binomial) probabilities. The lower panel records the sample variance, which follows the line $2kt$.

pde-3.4.name: Solution of the heat equation on the line by convolution
pde-3.4.statement:
Let $g$ be bounded and continuous on $\R$. Then
$$u(x,t)=(\Phi(\cdot,t)*g)(x)=\int_{\R}\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi kt}}\,e^{-(x-y)^2/(4kt)}\,g(y)\,dy,\qquad t>0,$$
is $C^\infty$ for $t>0$, solves $u_t=ku_{xx}$, and $u(x,t)\to g(x)$ as $(x,t)\to(x_0,0^+)$ at every point of continuity; it is the unique bounded solution with this initial value. The formula also makes sense (and gives a solution for $t>0$) for bounded piecewise-continuous $g$, taking the values $g(x_0\pm)$ averaged at jumps.
pde-3.4.caption: Draw the initial temperature with the mouse (drag across the left panel) or pick a preset; move time $t$ and diffusivity $k$. The solid blue curve is the convolution with the heat kernel (each data cell integrated against $\Phi$ exactly through the error function); the dashed orange one is an independent finite-difference solution (Crank–Nicolson after four backward-Euler start-up steps, cell size $0.05$) and the readout gives the largest difference. Drag the gold handle $x_0$: the lower panel shows the weight $\Phi(x_0-y,t)$ and the product with the data, whose area is $u(x_0,t)$.

music-8.1.name: Pitch classes and ℤ/12
music-8.1.statement: In twelve-tone equal temperament the notes are the MIDI numbers $m\in\Z$ (one per semitone). Two notes an octave apart, $m$ and $m+12$, are given the same **pitch class** $[m]=m \bmod 12\in\Z/12=\{0,1,\dots,11\}$ (0 = C, 1 = C♯/D♭, …, 11 = B). Pitch classes live on a **clock**: adding $n$ semitones is the rotation $x\mapsto x+n \pmod{12}$, so transposing a melody or chord rotates the whole picture rigidly, and everything that depends only on pitch classes (names of chords, scale types, interval content) is a statement about subsets of $\Z/12$.
music-8.1.caption: Click the clock to add or remove pitch classes of the chord, and slide $n$ to transpose it: the orange arcs show every note advancing $n$ hours. Below, the same notes are drawn in all octaves of a keyboard range; the transposed copy keeps the shape. The buttons play the chord and its transposition, or one pitch class in three octaves.

rep-1.1.name: Linear representations
rep-1.1.credit: Frobenius, 1896–97 (characters and representations of finite groups); developed independently by Burnside (1898) and Schur (1905)
rep-1.1.statement: A **(linear) representation** of a group $G$ on a vector space $V$ over a field $k$ is a homomorphism $\rho\colon G\to GL(V)$ into the group of invertible linear maps of $V$. Concretely, to each $g\in G$ is attached an invertible matrix $\rho(g)$ (after choosing a basis; $n=\dim V$ is the **degree**) such that $\rho(gh)=\rho(g)\,\rho(h)$ for all $g,h\in G$. This forces $\rho(e)=I$ and $\rho(g^{-1})=\rho(g)^{-1}$. The representation is **faithful** when $\rho$ is injective.
rep-1.1.caption: Pick the symmetry group of the triangle or the square, then click any cell of the multiplication table: the dashed figure is moved by $\rho(h)$ (orange), then by $\rho(g)$ (blue); the green outline is $\rho(gh)$. Green cells are products where $\rho(gh)=\rho(g)\rho(h)$ holds numerically. Now turn the "tamper" slider: it rotates the single matrix $\rho(s)$ off the symmetry it should be, and every product that involves $s$ turns red.

bridges.title: Least action: nature’s shortest paths
bridges.blurb: Light takes the quickest route, a falling bead the fastest slide, a planet the path of stationary action, and a free particle in curved spacetime the path of longest proper time. One principle runs from optics through mechanics and symmetry to relativity and quantum theory.

steps.name: Fermat’s principle and Snell’s law
steps.note: Fermat: light travels between two points along the path of least time. Snell's law of refraction follows from asking where to cross the boundary.

steps.name: Brachistochrone: the cycloid
steps.note: Johann Bernoulli's challenge, the curve of fastest descent, is a cycloid, and his solution borrowed Fermat's optics.

steps.name: Euler–Lagrange equation
steps.note: Euler and Lagrange turned such problems into a method: a path that makes an integral stationary must satisfy a differential equation.

steps.name: Hamilton’s principle of stationary action
steps.note: Hamilton's principle: the motion of any mechanical system makes the action $\int (T - V)\,dt$ stationary. Newton's laws become one variational statement.

steps.name: Noether’s theorem
steps.note: Noether's theorem: every continuous symmetry of the action gives a conserved quantity. Time symmetry gives energy, space symmetry momentum, rotation angular momentum.

steps.name: Maupertuis’ principle and the Jacobi metric
steps.note: Maupertuis and Jacobi: at fixed energy, orbits are geodesics of a modified metric. Dynamics becomes geometry.

steps.name: dg-9.7
steps.note: On a curved surface the shortest paths are geodesics, curves whose acceleration points straight out of the surface.

steps.name: rel-7.7
steps.note: In general relativity a freely falling body follows a timelike geodesic, the path that makes its own clock tick the most.

steps.name: rel-8.6
steps.note: Even the gravitational field obeys an action principle: varying the Einstein–Hilbert action gives Einstein's field equations.

steps.name: waves-5.2
steps.note: Why least time? Waves along nearby paths interfere; only near a stationary path do the phases agree and add up. Fermat's principle is stationary phase.

steps.name: Feynman path integral
steps.note: Feynman made that literal for matter: a particle takes every path, each weighted by $e^{iS/\hbar}$. When $S \gg \hbar$ all but the classical path cancel.

bridges.title: How things spread: epidemics, rumours and riots
bridges.blurb: A disease, a rumour, a fad and a bank run all spread from person to person, and the same mathematics decides whether they fizzle or explode: a threshold number of new cases per case, shaped by who is connected to whom.

steps.name: soc-5.8
steps.note: Start with a branching process: each case causes a random number of new ones. If the mean is below one the outbreak dies out for sure; above one it can run forever.

steps.name: mathbio-7.2
steps.note: That mean is the basic reproduction number $R_0$: new infections caused by one case in a fully susceptible population.

steps.name: mathbio-7.3
steps.note: Kermack and McKendrick's threshold theorem: an epidemic takes off exactly when $R_0 > 1$, and herd immunity begins at a fraction $1 - 1/R_0$ immune.

steps.name: mathbio-7.6
steps.note: Epidemics overshoot: infections keep coming after the herd-immunity point, so far more than $1 - 1/R_0$ end up infected.

steps.name: stoch-10.11
steps.note: With chance in the model, even an outbreak with $R_0 > 1$ can die out early; the probability of a major epidemic is the branching-process survival probability.

steps.name: mathbio-7.12
steps.note: Seasonal forcing of contact rates turns the damped waves of an endemic disease into the regular recurrent outbreaks seen in measles.

steps.name: The giant component appears at mean degree one
steps.note: On a random network a giant connected component appears suddenly at mean degree one: the same threshold, now as a phase transition in connectivity.

steps.name: soc-5.9
steps.note: On real networks heavy-tailed degrees lower the threshold: highly connected hubs keep an epidemic alive.

steps.name: Granovetter’s threshold model of collective behaviour
steps.note: Behaviour spreads differently. In Granovetter's model each person joins a riot once enough others have, and the outcome hinges on the whole distribution of thresholds.

steps.name: Fragile cascades: one changed threshold stops the riot
steps.note: Change one person's threshold and a riot of hundreds can collapse to a handful: cascades are fragile.

steps.name: soc-5.3
steps.note: Complex contagions need several exposures, so they spread through clustered, redundant ties rather than long-range shortcuts, the opposite of disease.

steps.name: soc-5.4
steps.note: Information cascades: rational people who follow others' choices instead of their private signals can lock a whole crowd into the wrong answer.

bridges.title: The random walk: from pollen grains to option prices
bridges.blurb: A particle kicked at random goes nowhere on average, yet spreads like $\sqrt t$. That one fact links Brown's jiggling pollen, the heat equation, Einstein's count of atoms, the size of living cells, the price of options and the image generators of modern AI.

steps.name: thermo-7.8
steps.note: In 1827 Robert Brown saw pollen grains jiggling in water, endlessly and for no visible reason.

steps.name: thermo-7.9
steps.note: A random walk of $n$ independent steps ends about $\sqrt n$ steps from home: displacement averages to zero, but its square grows linearly.

steps.name: thermo-7.10
steps.note: Einstein (1905) tied the spreading rate to temperature and friction, $D = \mu k T$, so watching the jiggling measures Boltzmann's constant and counts atoms.

steps.name: thermo-7.6
steps.note: Averaged over many walkers, randomness becomes a law: the flux runs down the concentration gradient, $J = -D\nabla c$.

steps.name: Diffusion and the heat equation
steps.note: Combined with conservation, Fick's law gives the diffusion (heat) equation $u_t = D\,\Delta u$: the same equation for heat, dye and probability.

steps.name: Solution of the heat equation on the line by convolution
steps.note: Its solution is a convolution with a spreading Gaussian, the probability cloud of a single random walker.

steps.name: stoch-13.2
steps.note: Donsker: rescaled random walks converge to one universal limit, Brownian motion, whatever the step distribution.

steps.name: stoch-13.5
steps.note: Its paths are continuous but nowhere differentiable: zoom in anywhere and they look just as rough.

steps.name: stoch-13.16
steps.note: Brownian motion solves boundary-value problems: the harmonic function at a point is the average boundary value where a walker started there first hits.

steps.name: mathbio-8.4
steps.note: Because the time to diffuse grows as length squared, diffusion is fast across a cell and hopeless across a body, one reason cells are small and animals have blood vessels.

steps.name: pde-9.8
steps.note: Add growth to diffusion and you get travelling fronts (Fisher–KPP): the spread of an advantageous gene or an invading species.

steps.name: stoch-13.14
steps.note: Let the walk be multiplicative and you get geometric Brownian motion, the standard model of a stock price.

steps.name: fin-9.3
steps.note: Black and Scholes priced an option on such a stock; a change of variables turns their equation into the heat equation.

steps.name: deep-10.10
steps.note: Diffusion models generate images by learning to run the process backwards, turning noise step by step into a picture.

bridges.title: Entropy: counting, ignorance and information
bridges.blurb: One formula, $-\sum p\ln p$, turned up three times: in steam engines, in the statistics of atoms, and in telephone lines. Following it shows why heat flows downhill, why erasing a bit costs energy, how compression works, and what a neural network minimizes when it learns.

steps.name: Second law: Kelvin–Planck and Clausius statements
steps.note: It starts with engines: no device can turn heat entirely into work, and heat never flows unaided from cold to hot. Two equivalent statements of one law.

steps.name: Entropy as a state function
steps.note: Clausius found the quantity that law protects: $dS = \delta q_{\text{rev}}/T$ adds up to the same total along every reversible path, so entropy is a property of the state.

steps.name: Boltzmann entropy
steps.note: Boltzmann explained what it counts: $S = k\ln W$, the logarithm of the number of microscopic arrangements that look the same from outside.

steps.name: The second law as overwhelming probability
steps.note: So the second law is a statement about odds: macrostates with more arrangements are overwhelmingly more likely, and for $10^{23}$ particles "overwhelmingly" means "always".

steps.name: Gibbs entropy
steps.note: When the microstates are not equally likely, Gibbs's version weights them: $S = -k\sum_i p_i \ln p_i$.

steps.name: Shannon entropy
steps.note: Shannon, studying telephone lines, needed a measure of surprise that adds over independent events, and arrived at the same expression in bits: $H = -\sum p\log_2 p$.

steps.name: Block coding approaches the entropy
steps.note: It is not just a definition: entropy is exactly the number of bits per symbol that the best compressor can reach, and no compressor can beat it.

steps.name: Maxwell’s demon
steps.note: Maxwell's demon seems to beat the second law by sorting fast and slow molecules. The resolution goes through information.

steps.name: Landauer’s principle
steps.note: Landauer: erasing one bit of memory dissipates at least $kT\ln 2$ of heat. The demon must forget what it measured, and the books balance.

steps.name: Maximum entropy principle
steps.note: Turned around, entropy becomes a rule of inference: assume nothing beyond what you know. Maximizing entropy at fixed mean energy gives the Boltzmann distribution.

steps.name: Relative entropy (Kullback–Leibler divergence)
steps.note: The relative entropy $D(p\|q)$ measures the cost of believing $q$ when the truth is $p$; it is never negative.

steps.name: Second law: divergence to equilibrium decreases
steps.note: In a Markov chain the divergence to the stationary distribution can only shrink: the second law, recast for any random process.

steps.name: Softmax and cross-entropy loss
steps.note: A classifier trained with cross-entropy loss is minimizing a divergence from the data: the same quantity, now steering gradient descent.

steps.name: qm-14.5
steps.note: In quantum mechanics the von Neumann entropy of part of a system measures its entanglement with the rest.

steps.name: rel-10.16
steps.note: And at the edge of physics, a black hole has entropy proportional to the area of its horizon, $S = kA/4\ell_P^2$: the largest entropy any region can hold.

bridges.title: Fixed points: where a map leaves something alone
bridges.blurb: Many existence proofs come down to one move: write the thing you want as a point that some map sends to itself, then show such a point must exist. That move proves differential equations have solutions, markets and games have equilibria, Google can rank the web, programs can print themselves, and light settles into a rendered image.

steps.name: Every self-map of an interval has a fixed point
steps.note: The simplest case: a continuous map of an interval to itself must cross the diagonal somewhere, by the intermediate value theorem.

steps.name: Contraction principle (Banach fixed point theorem)
steps.note: Banach's contraction principle: if a map shrinks every distance by a fixed factor, iterating it from anywhere converges to its unique fixed point, and you can say how fast.

steps.name: Picard–Lindelöf theorem
steps.note: Picard–Lindelöf: a solution of $x' = f(t,x)$ is a fixed point of the integral map $x \mapsto x_0 + \int f(s, x(s))\,ds$, which is a contraction on a short enough interval.

steps.name: Newton’s method
steps.note: Newton's method is fixed-point iteration for a cleverly chosen map whose fixed point is a root and whose derivative vanishes there, so the error squares at each step.

steps.name: top-13.11
steps.note: Brouwer: every continuous map of a ball to itself has a fixed point. Unlike Banach's theorem it gives no algorithm and no uniqueness, only existence.

steps.name: top-9.9
steps.note: Sperner's lemma, a counting fact about coloured triangulations, gives a combinatorial proof of Brouwer and a way to hunt for approximate fixed points.

steps.name: Nash’s existence theorem
steps.note: Nash: every finite game has an equilibrium in mixed strategies, a fixed point of the map that moves each player towards better replies.

steps.name: Existence of exchange equilibrium
steps.note: An exchange economy has prices that clear every market at once: the same topology, now applied to excess demand on the price simplex.

steps.name: Perron–Frobenius theorem
steps.note: Perron–Frobenius: a positive matrix has a positive eigenvector, a fixed direction, which gives the long-run distribution of a Markov chain.

steps.name: PageRank
steps.note: PageRank is that eigenvector for a random surfer on the web graph, found by iterating the map until it stops changing.

steps.name: Extinction probability is the least fixed point of the offspring PGF
steps.note: The extinction probability of a branching process is the smallest fixed point of its offspring generating function.

steps.name: logic-7.5
steps.note: In logic the diagonal lemma builds, for any property, a sentence that asserts it has that property. Gödel's sentence is such a fixed point.

steps.name: toc-11.2
steps.note: Kleene's recursion theorem: every computable transformation of programs fixes the behaviour of some program, which is why quines exist.

steps.name: Fixed-point combinators and recursion
steps.note: In the λ-calculus fixed-point combinators such as $Y$ produce recursion out of nothing.

steps.name: cg-11.3
steps.note: The rendering equation describes light as a fixed point: outgoing light equals emitted light plus reflected incoming light. Path tracing iterates the contraction.

bridges.title: Fourier: one idea, many fields
bridges.blurb: Breaking a signal into pure frequencies began as a tool for heat flow. It became the analyst's theory of orthogonal expansions, the physicist's resonance, the musician's timbre, the engineer's sampling theorem and the computer scientist's fastest algorithm.

steps.name: Orthonormal systems and Fourier coefficients
steps.note: A periodic function is projected onto sines and cosines; each coefficient measures how much of one frequency the function contains.

steps.name: Partial Fourier sums are the best mean-square approximations
steps.note: Truncating the series gives the best approximation in the mean-square sense, which is why a few harmonics already capture most of a shape.

steps.name: Parseval's theorem
steps.note: Parseval: the energy of the function equals the sum of the energies of its harmonics. Nothing is lost in the translation to frequencies.

steps.name: Fourier transform of an L¹ function
steps.note: Non-periodic signals get a continuous spectrum: the Fourier transform replaces the sum over harmonics with an integral over all frequencies.

steps.name: The Plancherel theorem
steps.note: Plancherel extends the transform to every finite-energy signal and keeps energy exactly, making it a rotation of $L^2$.

steps.name: Fourier analysis of periodic driving
steps.note: A driven oscillator responds to each harmonic of a periodic force separately; resonance picks out the harmonic closest to the natural frequency.

steps.name: The harmonic series
steps.note: A vibrating string supports only whole-number multiples of its fundamental: the harmonic series is a Fourier series that nature plays.

steps.name: Fourier series of a periodic tone
steps.note: What distinguishes a violin from a flute on the same note is the set of Fourier coefficients: timbre is a spectrum.

steps.name: Parseval: a tone’s energy is the sum over harmonics
steps.note: Parseval again, now audible: the loudness of a tone is shared among its harmonics.

steps.name: sig-7.3
steps.note: The sampling theorem: a signal with no frequencies above $B$ is completely determined by samples taken $2B$ times a second. Digital audio rests on it.

steps.name: Fast Fourier transform (Cooley–Tukey)
steps.note: The fast Fourier transform computes $n$ frequency components in $O(n\log n)$ steps instead of $O(n^2)$, by halving the problem with roots of unity.

steps.name: Integer multiplication via the FFT
steps.note: Multiplying two huge integers is a convolution of their digits, and convolution is multiplication of spectra: the FFT turns arithmetic into signal processing.

bridges.title: The spectral theorem: finding the natural axes
bridges.blurb: Every symmetric operator has a set of perpendicular directions in which it simply stretches. That single fact explains the principal axes of a spinning body, the normal modes of a vibrating system, the harmonics of a string and the shape of data.

steps.name: Eigenvalue
steps.note: An eigenvalue is a number $\lambda$ with $Tv = \lambda v$ for some nonzero $v$: a direction the operator only stretches.

steps.name: Eigenvalues of self-adjoint operators are real
steps.note: For a self-adjoint operator every eigenvalue is real, so the stretching factors are genuine lengths, not rotations.

steps.name: Real spectral theorem
steps.note: The real spectral theorem: a self-adjoint operator has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors. In that basis its matrix is diagonal.

steps.name: Ellipsoid with principal axes
steps.note: Geometrically, a positive operator maps the unit sphere to an ellipsoid whose principal axes are the eigenvectors.

steps.name: Singular value decomposition
steps.note: The singular value decomposition does the same for any operator: rotate, stretch along perpendicular axes, rotate again.

steps.name: The spectral theorem for normal operators
steps.note: In infinite dimensions the eigenvectors may not exist, but a projection-valued measure takes their place: the spectral theorem for normal operators.

steps.name: Principal axes of inertia
steps.note: The inertia tensor of a rigid body is symmetric; its eigenvectors are the principal axes, about which the body can spin without wobbling.

steps.name: Normal modes: the generalized eigenvalue problem
steps.note: Small oscillations of coupled masses decouple into normal modes, the solutions of a generalized eigenvalue problem; each mode swings at its own frequency.

steps.name: Standing waves and normal modes
steps.note: A string or a drum is a system with infinitely many normal modes: its standing waves are eigenfunctions of the wave operator.

bridges.title: Symmetry: from wallpaper to conservation laws
bridges.blurb: A symmetry is a transformation that leaves something unchanged, and the symmetries of anything form a group. That single idea classifies wallpaper and crystals, counts necklaces, organizes musical scales, predicts which molecular vibrations absorb light, and lies behind every conservation law in physics.

steps.name: art-9.1
steps.note: Every rigid motion of the plane is a translation, rotation, reflection or glide reflection.

steps.name: art-9.3
steps.note: The motions that leave a pattern unchanged form its symmetry group: composing two symmetries gives another, and each can be undone.

steps.name: art-9.6
steps.note: Patterns repeating in one direction come in exactly seven kinds: the frieze groups seen on every border and railing.

steps.name: art-9.9
steps.note: Patterns repeating in two directions come in exactly seventeen, the wallpaper groups, all found in the Alhambra's tiles.

steps.name: The fourteen Bravais lattices
steps.note: In three dimensions, the regular arrangements of points are the fourteen Bravais lattices; atoms in crystals sit on them.

steps.name: The 230 space groups
steps.note: Combining lattices with rotations and reflections gives the 230 space groups, the complete list of crystal symmetries.

steps.name: comb-10.4
steps.note: Groups also count: the number of different necklaces is the average number of colourings each rotation leaves fixed (Burnside's lemma).

steps.name: Pitch classes and ℤ/12
steps.note: Music has its symmetries too: pitch classes form the cyclic group $\mathbb Z/12$, with transposition as addition and inversion as negation.

steps.name: Linear representations
steps.note: A representation lets a group act by matrices, so linear algebra can be used to study symmetry.

steps.name: Orthogonality of irreducible characters
steps.note: Characters, the traces of those matrices, are orthogonal; a small table of numbers captures every representation of a finite group.

steps.name: qchem-8.9
steps.note: For a molecule, decomposing its motion into irreducible representations of its point group counts the normal modes of each symmetry type.

steps.name: qchem-8.10
steps.note: Only modes with the right symmetry can absorb infrared light or scatter Raman light: selection rules read straight off the character table.

steps.name: Noether’s theorem
steps.note: In mechanics, Noether's theorem turns continuous symmetries into conservation laws.

steps.name: Isotropy of space: conservation of angular momentum
steps.note: Space looks the same in every direction, so angular momentum is conserved.

steps.name: Angular momentum generates rotations
steps.note: In quantum mechanics angular momentum generates rotations, and its allowed values are fixed by the representations of the rotation group.

steps.name: rep-8.10
steps.note: The irreducible representations of $SO(3)$ are the spherical harmonics, which give the shapes of atomic orbitals: s, p, d and f.
